newsitem.title: CHINA: China warns U.S. against revoking MFN status.
newsitem.headline: China warns U.S. against revoking MFN status.

text.p: China warned on Thursday that the United States would have more to lose if it decided not to renew Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status for Beijing.
"If MFN were cancelled...the United States will be hurt as a result," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing.
"I believe U.S. losses will be very big," Shen said.
House of Representatives Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt said on Wednesday he would likely oppose renewal of MFN to China this year -- as he did last year.
Shen said renewal of MFN status, which gives China the same access to U.S. markets as most other trading nations, would help trade and other ties.
"On the issue of MFN, China is not the one that should be worried. The United States is the one that should be worried," the spokesman said.
"Renewing MFN...conforms with the interests of the two countries."

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said in Grand Rapids, Michigan, on Wednesday she expected President Bill Clinton to seek renewal of MFN trading status for China, saying it would promote human rights there.
Clinton has until June to decide whether to renew Beijing's MFN status. Congress then must decide whether to accept MFN renewal or vote to revoke it.

Many trade analysts have said they expect a tough fight on the matter in Congress because of concerns about human rights abuses, nuclear techonology sales and allegations that Beijing tried to influence U.S. elections through illegal campaign contributions.
Albright said the United States had a "strategic relationship with China that needs to be nurtured".

"As far as Most Favoured Nation for China, we are obviously going to be pressing in order to make sure that that is renewed. We believe that it is important for us to have a trading relationship with China," Albright said.
She said the debate on the MFN issue in the United States had basically set human rights against trade, but added that these two were not necessarily contradictory.
"If we can have a good trade relationship with China, it creates an atmosphere where it is more likely that human rights and political freedom will be respected in China," she said.
